transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Nice to meet you. Well, I guess... the main reason I made the appointment is that lately, my head has just been feeling incredibly foggy. And I mean, like, walking through thick mud kind of foggy, if that makes sense. I work as a personal care aide, you see, so I'm constantly juggling different tasks for my clients—helping them out, keeping track of their daily routines, that sort of thing—and I usually have a really good handle on all of it. I even took a few college classes back in the day that really helped with my organizational skills, so I'm usually very meticulous. 

But recently, I'm just... I'm making these little mistakes in my client notes. Like, I'll write down the wrong detail, or I'll walk into the kitchen to grab something for one of my guys and just stand there completely forgetting what I was about to do. And that really, really isn't like me at all. I'm usually very sharp, very on top of things, because in my line of work, you really have to be, you know? If I mess up a note, it could throw off the person coming in for the next shift, so it's been really weighing on me, this whole... cloudiness up there. I just can't seem to shake it, and I'm not used to feeling this scattered.
Can you tell me about your sleep lately—are you having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up feeling unrefreshed?

Oh, my sleep. Yeah, that's... well, it's really been all over the place lately, to be completely honest with you. It's just a mess. It's like I get into bed, right? And I do all the things you're supposed to do—make sure the room is quiet, get comfortable—but then I just lie there. And my brain just decides it's the perfect time to start thinking about all this family stuff we have going on. Like, my parents are getting older, and I start worrying about if I'm doing enough for them, or checking in on my sister, and I just turn it over and over in my head. Before I know it, an hour has gone by, maybe two, just staring in the dark. 

So falling asleep is definitely a struggle. But then, even when I finally do manage to drift off, it's not like I'm getting a good, solid night of rest. I'll wake up way before my alarm is even supposed to go off. I usually set it for 5:30 AM because I like to get a head start before I head over to my first client's house, but lately I'll find myself wide awake at, like, 3:45 or 4:00 in the morning. And I try to just close my eyes and breathe and tell myself to go back to sleep, but I just can't really settle back down. I just lie there looking at the ceiling, thinking about the family stuff all over again, or just getting frustrated that I'm awake. So I guess you could say it's both—trouble falling asleep and staying asleep. It's exhausting, really, especially when you know you need to be sharp for the people you're taking care of the next day.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed a change in your mood—like feeling down, sad, or losing interest or pleasure in things you normally enjoy?

Well, yeah, actually... it's funny you bring that up, because I've been thinking about that a lot. Over the past couple of weeks, maybe even a little longer, it's just... it's like I wake up, and even before I get out of bed, there's this heavy, empty feeling sitting right in the middle of my chest. It's hard to explain, but it's just this weight. And I get up, you know, I make my coffee, I get dressed, I drive over to my clients' houses, and I can still do the job. I mean, I can smile, I can make small talk with Mrs. Higgins about her garden, I can go through all the motions of getting them bathed and fed and everything. 

But the whole time, it's like I'm just acting. Inside, I just feel so sad. Just really, really flat. Like the color has sort of washed out of everything. I used to really look forward to my weekends—I'd go down to the hardware store, maybe putter around in the garage, or watch the game with my buddy Dave. But lately, even the thought of doing any of that just feels... I don't know, exhausting? Pointless? I just don't have the energy or the desire for it. I just sit on the couch and stare at the TV without really watching it. It's just this constant, low-level sadness that I can't seem to shake off, no matter how much I try to just push through it and focus on my work. It's just always there, right beneath the surface, making everything feel like such a chore.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight, or things like feeling unusually cold, dry skin, or hair thinning over the past couple of months?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I haven't noticed any major changes in my weight, honestly. I still pretty much eat the same things I always do—mostly sandwiches when I'm on the go between clients, maybe a bowl of soup or something easy when I get home because I'm just too tired to really cook a big meal. But my clothes all fit exactly the same, my belts are on the same notch, so I don't think I've gained or lost anything noticeable. 

And as for feeling cold, I don't think so. I mean, my apartment gets a little drafty in the winter because it's an older building, and sometimes the radiator clanks and doesn't put out as much heat as I'd like, but that's just normal for the place, you know? It's not like I'm shivering all the time or wearing a coat indoors or anything like that. I'm usually pretty comfortable. 

And my skin and hair... well, I've always had kind of normal skin, I guess. I use a little lotion in the winter when the air gets dry, especially on my hands because I wash them so much at work—you know, hygiene is huge when you're a personal care aide, you're constantly washing up before and after you help someone. But it's not unusually dry or anything. And my hair is fine, too. I mean, I'm 43, so maybe it's not as thick as it was when I was in my twenties taking those college classes, but it's not falling out in clumps or thinning in any new or weird way. So, yeah, I'd have to say no to all of that. Just the same old me in that department, really.

Would you say this pattern of worrying excessively about several different things—not just your family—has been happening on most days for the past six months or longer, and that it's hard for you to control or stop the worry once it starts?

Well, I wouldn't really say it's been going on for six months, no. And I wouldn't say it's about everything, either. I mean, sure, I worry, who doesn't? But it's not like this constant, everyday thing where I'm just agonizing over every little detail of my life for half the year. 

It's really just the family stuff, mostly. Like I mentioned, with my parents getting older, that's the big one. My dad had that scare with his heart a while back, and ever since then, it's just always in the back of my mind. And my sister, she lives a couple of states over, so I don't get to see her much, and I worry if she's doing okay, if she's stressed with her kids. But it's not like I'm sitting there worrying about my job security, or if my car is going to break down, or if the economy is going to crash, or anything like that. I'm pretty practical about all that stuff. 

And as for it being hard to control... I mean, when I'm lying in bed, yeah, the thoughts kind of loop around, but during the day, I can usually just focus on my clients. When I'm at Mrs. Higgins' place, I'm thinking about her medications and making sure she eats, not just obsessing over my own stuff. So, no, it's not this out-of-control, all-the-time worry about a million different things for the last six months. It's just... you know, the normal amount of stress when you care about your family, just maybe hitting me a little harder lately because of how tired and down I've been feeling. But definitely not what you're describing.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms like feeling unusually short of breath, lightheaded, or dizzy, or has anyone commented that you look pale, over these past couple of months?

No, I haven't really had anything like that. I mean, my job is pretty physical, you know? Being a personal care aide, I'm constantly on my feet and moving around. Take Mr. Henderson, for example—he's one of my afternoon clients, and he lives up on the third floor of this older walk-up building. The elevator there has been broken for, I don't know, maybe three or four weeks now? The landlord is dragging his feet on fixing it. Anyway, I have to carry his groceries up all those stairs. I get to the top and I'm breathing a little hard, sure, but just the normal amount for a 43-year-old guy carrying two heavy bags of canned goods and a gallon of milk. It's not like I'm gasping for air or feeling unusually winded when I'm just sitting around or walking on flat ground. My breathing is totally fine.

And as for feeling dizzy or lightheaded... no, not at all. I really have to be steady on my feet for my job, because I'm helping people transfer from their beds to their wheelchairs, or getting them into the shower. If I was getting dizzy, that would be a huge liability. I mean, imagine if I got lightheaded while helping Mrs. Higgins into the bath—we could both go down and get seriously hurt, and at her age, a fall is catastrophic. But thankfully, my balance is rock solid. I never get that spinning feeling or feel like I'm going to pass out, not even if I stand up really fast from the couch. 

And looking pale? No, no one's said anything like that to me. I mean, I see my buddy Dave sometimes, and even though I haven't been as into hanging out or watching the game lately, he still drops by, and he's the kind of guy who has absolutely no filter. If I looked sick or washed out, he'd be the first one to say, "Whoa, man, you look like a ghost," or something like that. But he hasn't mentioned a thing. I look in the mirror when I shave every morning, and I just look like my regular self. I mean, maybe my eyes look a little tired just because I've been feeling so dragged down and heavy on the inside lately, but my skin color is completely normal. I'm definitely not pale. So yeah, I haven't had any of those physical issues you're talking about, just the mood stuff.

Thinking back, did you notice the mental fogginess and memory slips starting around the same time as the low mood and sleep trouble, or did the foggy thinking actually begin first, before you started feeling down?

Well, let me think about that. It’s actually... they really kind of all rolled in together, to be honest. It wasn't like I woke up one day and just couldn't remember things, and then a week later started feeling sad. No, it’s all been this one big package deal. The whole thing—this low, guilty, foggy feeling—has just been hanging over me for about a month now. 

I can trace it back to right around four weeks ago, maybe a little over, when I was covering a few extra shifts because one of the other aides caught that nasty bug that was going around. I remember it clearly because I was just feeling so incredibly sluggish and down, and at the exact same time, my brain started feeling like it was stuffed with cotton. Like, I’d be looking at Mrs. Higgins' daily pill organizer, and I’d have to check it three times because the mental fog was so thick. And then, almost instantly, I’d get hit with this massive wave of guilt, feeling like I’m a terrible caregiver for not being sharp, which just made my mood tank even further. 

So they definitely feed into each other, you know? It’s not one starting before the other. It’s just been this solid month of dragging myself around, feeling bad about myself, and struggling to keep my thoughts straight all at the exact same time. Like just the other day, I was at the grocery store picking up supplies for Mr. Henderson, and I stood in the cereal aisle for what felt like ten minutes just staring at the oatmeal because I couldn't process which brand he usually likes. And of course, standing there, I just felt so guilty and useless that I couldn't remember a simple thing like that, which just made that heavy, low feeling in my chest even worse. So yeah, definitely all starting up together about a month ago, just this one big cloud I can't seem to shake.
Have you noticed any new digestive issues, such as constipation, or unusual muscle aches or joint stiffness, over the past couple of months?

Well, no, my stomach has been totally fine. Actually, I am pretty regular. Working in home care, you really start to pay attention to digestion because for a lot of my older clients, that is a huge part of their daily struggle. Take Mr. Henderson, he is always dealing with constipation, so I am constantly making sure he gets enough fiber, mixing up these bran and prune concoctions for him. And honestly, because I am making those meals for them, I end up eating pretty well myself. I will have a bowl of oatmeal right along with Mrs. Higgins in the morning, and I make sure I drink plenty of water throughout the day because it gets so stuffy in those older apartments. So absolutely no issues on the bathroom front for me. Everything is working exactly like it always has. 

And as for the muscle aches or joint stiffness, no, not at all. Like I was saying earlier about carrying those groceries up all those stairs, my job is basically a workout. If I had stiff joints, I just would not be able to do it. I am constantly bending down to tie shoes, reaching up to grab things from high cabinets, helping people pivot from a chair to a walker. You would think maybe my back would hurt from all that lifting, but I learned proper body mechanics back when I took my aide certification classes at the community college. They really drill that into you, lifting with your legs and not your back, keeping your core tight. 

So my muscles feel fine. I mean, sure, at the end of a long shift my feet might be a little tired, but just the regular kind of tired, you know? It is not like I am waking up stiff or having unusual aches or pains out of nowhere. My body actually feels completely normal physically. It is really just that mental heaviness and the mood that has been dragging me down, definitely not my stomach or my joints.

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Lately I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling in my chest, like I can get through my shift and talk to people but inside I’m just sad and flat.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling down, sad, or losing interest, which directly maps to the Depressed_Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, actually... it's funny you bring that up, because I've been thinking about that a lot. Over the past couple of weeks, maybe even a little longer, it's just... it's like I wake up, and even before I get out of bed, there's this heavy, empty feeling sitting right in the middle of my chest. It's hard to explain, but it's just this weight. And I get up, you know, I make my coffee, I get dressed, I drive over to my clients' houses, and I can still do the job. I mean, I can smile, I can make small talk with Mrs. Higgins about her garden, I can go through all the motions of getting them bathed and fed and everything. 

But the whole time, it's like I'm just acting. Inside, I just feel so sad. Just really, really flat. Like the color has sort of washed out of everything. I used to really look forward to my weekends—I'd go down to the hardware store, maybe putter around in the garage, or watch the game with my buddy Dave. But lately, even the thought of doing any of that just feels... I don't know, exhausting? Pointless? I just don't have the energy or the desire for it. I just sit on the couch and stare at the TV without really watching it. It's just this constant, low-level sadness that I can't seem to shake off, no matter how much I try to just push through it and focus on my work. It's just always there, right beneath the surface, making everything feel like such a chore.

inference.note: Removed G47.9 as primary sleep disorder—insomnia pattern (early waking, rumination) appears secondary to mood/anxiety symptoms rather than a primary sleep disorder. Depressive symptoms (anhedonia, low mood, guilt-tinged rumination, cognitive fog) strengthen support for F32.9, while ongoing worry supports F41.1. Medical mimics (E03.9, D64.9) and organic cognitive disorder (F06.7) remain open pending labs/exam.

doctor.intent: Screen for physical/medical symptoms (e.g., weight change, cold intolerance, dry skin, fatigue) that might suggest an underlying thyroid or metabolic cause for the mood and cognitive changes
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your weight, or things like feeling unusually cold, dry skin, or hair thinning over the past couple of months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of hypothyroidism (weight changes, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair thinning), which are not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I mean, I haven't noticed any major changes in my weight, honestly. I still pretty much eat the same things I always do—mostly sandwiches when I'm on the go between clients, maybe a bowl of soup or something easy when I get home because I'm just too tired to really cook a big meal. But my clothes all fit exactly the same, my belts are on the same notch, so I don't think I've gained or lost anything noticeable. 

And as for feeling cold, I don't think so. I mean, my apartment gets a little drafty in the winter because it's an older building, and sometimes the radiator clanks and doesn't put out as much heat as I'd like, but that's just normal for the place, you know? It's not like I'm shivering all the time or wearing a coat indoors or anything like that. I'm usually pretty comfortable. 

And my skin and hair... well, I've always had kind of normal skin, I guess. I use a little lotion in the winter when the air gets dry, especially on my hands because I wash them so much at work—you know, hygiene is huge when you're a personal care aide, you're constantly washing up before and after you help someone. But it's not unusually dry or anything. And my hair is fine, too. I mean, I'm 43, so maybe it's not as thick as it was when I was in my twenties taking those college classes, but it's not falling out in clumps or thinning in any new or weird way. So, yeah, I'd have to say no to all of that. Just the same old me in that department, really.

inference.note: Patient denies classic hypothyroid symptoms (no weight change, cold intolerance, dry skin/hair changes), making E03.9 less likely but not excluded pending labs. Adjustment disorder (F43.20) is less consistent given the pervasive, syndromal quality of depressed mood, anhedonia, and vegetative symptoms (early morning awakening, anergia) persisting beyond a clear stressor-limited reaction, so it was removed. Core picture still supports MDD (F32.9) with prominent anxious rumination (F41.1) and cognitive complaints that could reflect either the mood/anxiety disorder itself or an underlying medical contributor (hypothyroidism, anemia) causing mild cognitive disturbance (F06.7).

doctor.intent: Determine whether the excessive worry is chronic, pervasive across multiple areas of life, and hard to control (key GAD criteria) versus limited to the recent low mood episode
doctor.question: Would you say this pattern of worrying excessively about several different things—not just your family—has been happening on most days for the past six months or longer, and that it's hard for you to control or stop the worry once it starts?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (excessive, uncontrollable worry over multiple things for 6+ months), which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't really say it's been going on for six months, no. And I wouldn't say it's about everything, either. I mean, sure, I worry, who doesn't? But it's not like this constant, everyday thing where I'm just agonizing over every little detail of my life for half the year. 

It's really just the family stuff, mostly. Like I mentioned, with my parents getting older, that's the big one. My dad had that scare with his heart a while back, and ever since then, it's just always in the back of my mind. And my sister, she lives a couple of states over, so I don't get to see her much, and I worry if she's doing okay, if she's stressed with her kids. But it's not like I'm sitting there worrying about my job security, or if my car is going to break down, or if the economy is going to crash, or anything like that. I'm pretty practical about all that stuff. 

And as for it being hard to control... I mean, when I'm lying in bed, yeah, the thoughts kind of loop around, but during the day, I can usually just focus on my clients. When I'm at Mrs. Higgins' place, I'm thinking about her medications and making sure she eats, not just obsessing over my own stuff. So, no, it's not this out-of-control, all-the-time worry about a million different things for the last six months. It's just... you know, the normal amount of stress when you care about your family, just maybe hitting me a little harder lately because of how tired and down I've been feeling. But definitely not what you're describing.

inference.note: GAD (F41.1) ruled out: worry is limited to family/parental health concerns, not pervasive across multiple domains, not present for 6+ months, and patient reports ability to control/focus away from it during work. Hypothyroid symptoms (weight change, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair thinning) are absent, lowering likelihood of E03.9 but not fully excluding it without labs. Depressive symptoms (anhedonia, low mood, fatigue, sleep disturbance, cognitive fog) support F32.9, while persistent cognitive complaints keep F06.7 and anemia (D64.9) as differentials pending labs.

doctor.intent: Assess for physical signs of anemia (e.g., fatigue disproportionate to sleep loss, shortness of breath, dizziness, pale skin) that could explain the cognitive fog
doctor.question: Have you noticed any physical symptoms like feeling unusually short of breath, lightheaded, or dizzy, or has anyone commented that you look pale, over these past couple of months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical symptoms like shortness of breath, lightheadedness, dizziness, and pallor, which are typically used to screen for medical conditions like anemia. These are not covered in my psychiatric symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't really had anything like that. I mean, my job is pretty physical, you know? Being a personal care aide, I'm constantly on my feet and moving around. Take Mr. Henderson, for example—he's one of my afternoon clients, and he lives up on the third floor of this older walk-up building. The elevator there has been broken for, I don't know, maybe three or four weeks now? The landlord is dragging his feet on fixing it. Anyway, I have to carry his groceries up all those stairs. I get to the top and I'm breathing a little hard, sure, but just the normal amount for a 43-year-old guy carrying two heavy bags of canned goods and a gallon of milk. It's not like I'm gasping for air or feeling unusually winded when I'm just sitting around or walking on flat ground. My breathing is totally fine.

And as for feeling dizzy or lightheaded... no, not at all. I really have to be steady on my feet for my job, because I'm helping people transfer from their beds to their wheelchairs, or getting them into the shower. If I was getting dizzy, that would be a huge liability. I mean, imagine if I got lightheaded while helping Mrs. Higgins into the bath—we could both go down and get seriously hurt, and at her age, a fall is catastrophic. But thankfully, my balance is rock solid. I never get that spinning feeling or feel like I'm going to pass out, not even if I stand up really fast from the couch. 

And looking pale? No, no one's said anything like that to me. I mean, I see my buddy Dave sometimes, and even though I haven't been as into hanging out or watching the game lately, he still drops by, and he's the kind of guy who has absolutely no filter. If I looked sick or washed out, he'd be the first one to say, "Whoa, man, you look like a ghost," or something like that. But he hasn't mentioned a thing. I look in the mirror when I shave every morning, and I just look like my regular self. I mean, maybe my eyes look a little tired just because I've been feeling so dragged down and heavy on the inside lately, but my skin color is completely normal. I'm definitely not pale. So yeah, I haven't had any of those physical issues you're talking about, just the mood stuff.

inference.note: Ruled out D64.9 (anemia) given no shortness of breath, dizziness, or pallor reported. GAD (F41.1) is not supported since worry is limited to family issues, not pervasive/multiple domains, and doesn't meet 6-month duration or uncontrollability criteria. Continuing to consider major depressive disorder (F32.9) given clear depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive fog; hypothyroidism (E03.9) remains possible cause of fatigue/cognitive slowing though some symptoms (cold intolerance, weight change) are absent; mild cognitive disorder due to another medical condition (F06.7) remains open given prominent cognitive complaints.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the cognitive fog/memory problems started before, at the same time as, or after the mood/sleep changes, to see if it's a primary cognitive disorder or secondary to depression
doctor.question: Thinking back, did you notice the mental fogginess and memory slips starting around the same time as the low mood and sleep trouble, or did the foggy thinking actually begin first, before you started feeling down?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The low, guilty, foggy feeling has been hanging over me for about a month now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline of the cognitive symptoms (foggy thinking) relative to the low mood, which is addressed by the depressive episode duration that groups the low and foggy feelings together over the past month.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think about that. It’s actually... they really kind of all rolled in together, to be honest. It wasn't like I woke up one day and just couldn't remember things, and then a week later started feeling sad. No, it’s all been this one big package deal. The whole thing—this low, guilty, foggy feeling—has just been hanging over me for about a month now. 

I can trace it back to right around four weeks ago, maybe a little over, when I was covering a few extra shifts because one of the other aides caught that nasty bug that was going around. I remember it clearly because I was just feeling so incredibly sluggish and down, and at the exact same time, my brain started feeling like it was stuffed with cotton. Like, I’d be looking at Mrs. Higgins' daily pill organizer, and I’d have to check it three times because the mental fog was so thick. And then, almost instantly, I’d get hit with this massive wave of guilt, feeling like I’m a terrible caregiver for not being sharp, which just made my mood tank even further. 

So they definitely feed into each other, you know? It’s not one starting before the other. It’s just been this solid month of dragging myself around, feeling bad about myself, and struggling to keep my thoughts straight all at the exact same time. Like just the other day, I was at the grocery store picking up supplies for Mr. Henderson, and I stood in the cereal aisle for what felt like ten minutes just staring at the oatmeal because I couldn't process which brand he usually likes. And of course, standing there, I just felt so guilty and useless that I couldn't remember a simple thing like that, which just made that heavy, low feeling in my chest even worse. So yeah, definitely all starting up together about a month ago, just this one big cloud I can't seem to shake.

inference.note: GAD ruled out - worry is limited to family topic, not excessive/uncontrollable across domains, and doesn't meet 6-month duration. Cardiopulmonary/anemia symptoms (dyspnea, dizziness, pallor) ruled out, making E03.9 less likely but still retained pending labs. Cognitive fog and depressive symptoms have concurrent onset (~1 month), consistent with pseudodementia from MDD (F32.9) or hypothyroidism-related cognitive slowing (E03.9); F06.7 (mild cognitive disorder due to medical condition) remains possible pending organic workup.

doctor.intent: Assess for additional classic hypothyroid symptoms (e.g., constipation, muscle aches, or menstrual changes) that haven't yet been explored, to help differentiate a thyroid-related cause from primary depression.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any new digestive issues, such as constipation, or unusual muscle aches or joint stiffness, over the past couple of months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical symptoms like constipation, muscle aches, or joint stiffness, which are not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Well, no, my stomach has been totally fine. Actually, I am pretty regular. Working in home care, you really start to pay attention to digestion because for a lot of my older clients, that is a huge part of their daily struggle. Take Mr. Henderson, he is always dealing with constipation, so I am constantly making sure he gets enough fiber, mixing up these bran and prune concoctions for him. And honestly, because I am making those meals for them, I end up eating pretty well myself. I will have a bowl of oatmeal right along with Mrs. Higgins in the morning, and I make sure I drink plenty of water throughout the day because it gets so stuffy in those older apartments. So absolutely no issues on the bathroom front for me. Everything is working exactly like it always has. 

And as for the muscle aches or joint stiffness, no, not at all. Like I was saying earlier about carrying those groceries up all those stairs, my job is basically a workout. If I had stiff joints, I just would not be able to do it. I am constantly bending down to tie shoes, reaching up to grab things from high cabinets, helping people pivot from a chair to a walker. You would think maybe my back would hurt from all that lifting, but I learned proper body mechanics back when I took my aide certification classes at the community college. They really drill that into you, lifting with your legs and not your back, keeping your core tight. 

So my muscles feel fine. I mean, sure, at the end of a long shift my feet might be a little tired, but just the regular kind of tired, you know? It is not like I am waking up stiff or having unusual aches or pains out of nowhere. My body actually feels completely normal physically. It is really just that mental heaviness and the mood that has been dragging me down, definitely not my stomach or my joints.

inference.note: Ruled out F06.7 (no medical/neurological cause found; no fatigue, joint/muscle symptoms, or other findings suggesting another medical condition) and E03.9 (denies cold intolerance, weight change, dry skin, or hair thinning, arguing against hypothyroidism). Symptoms of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disturbance with early waking, and concentration difficulty all emerged together about a month ago, consistent with a major depressive episode.
